**Short answer:** The projectors are almost certainly **above the performers**, rigged high and angled down. There appear to be **two of them**, one on each side of the stage, with their images overlapping on the back wall. I can't see the projectors themselves, so this is inferred from the shadows.

**Why above rather than below**

- **The shadows fall low on the wall.** In the wide shots (about 84–89 s, 184–186 s, 226–229 s), the performers' shadows sit low on the wall, near floor level or behind the amps and drum risers. The upper part of the wall shows the clouds, stars or lightning without interruption.
- **The clearest example is the tambourine player behind the lava-lamp stand** (about 167–173 s and 217–220 s). Her shadow sits beside her, level with or below her body, not above her.
- **A projector below would do the opposite.** A light near the floor pointing upward would throw large, stretched shadows that tower above the performers onto the image. Nothing like that appears. A high projector aimed down pushes shadows downward, where the band and equipment largely hide them.

**Why two projectors, one on each side**

- **Shadows fall in opposite directions.** The tambourine player's shadow is thrown down and to the left, so that light is coming from above and to the right.
- **The keyboard close-ups show the reverse.** At about 32–37 s, 93–95 s and 104–106 s, a round head-and-afro shadow appears low on the pale panel to the right of Prince. That light is coming from above and to the left.
- **The shadows are faint.** They are soft and partly washed out rather than solid black. That is what happens when a second projector, aimed from the other side, fills in the shadow cast by the first.

So the evidence points to two projectors mounted up in the lighting grid, one stage-left and one stage-right. Each casts shadows downward and toward the opposite side, and together they keep the upper wall image mostly shadow-free.

- The performers cast shadows onto the projected clouds, stars and lightning. With rear projection the image would come through the screen and nobody would cast a shadow on it.

# Where the projectors are, and how many of them there are

## The short answer

The projectors are off-screen **above** the performers. They are rigged overhead — up in the
lighting grid / on the studio truss, out of the top of frame and in front of the band — and they
are aimed downwards and backwards onto the back wall of the set. They are definitely not below the
performers and not at floor level.

There are **two** of them. One sits up and to the left of the stage centre-line and one up and to
the right, and their two images overlap in the middle of the wall so that together they cover the
full width of the set. Everything in this answer is measured off the video itself; the frame
timings quoted are seconds from the start of the 240.1 s file.

## Why the projectors must be above, not below

**The shadows fall below the objects that make them.** The clearest single piece of evidence is at
about t = 34–37 s, on the left of frame, where a performer in a silver sequinned sleeve is standing
close to the brightly cloud-lit wall. Immediately to the right of the sleeve, and displaced
*downwards*, there is a large, clean, hard-edged dark shape on the wall whose outline repeats the
shoulder and the arm. Because that dark shape lands *lower* on the wall than the arm that produced
it, the light making it has to be coming from a point *higher* than the arm. If a projector were
sitting below the performers, the same arm would throw its shadow *upwards* and the silhouette
would appear *above* the real arm on the wall. That never happens anywhere in the video — not one
up-raked shadow appears in 240 seconds.

**That shadow is a hole in the projected picture, not just a hole in the stage lighting.** This
matters, because a shadow from an ordinary stage lamp would tell us where the *lamp* is, not where
the *projector* is. Inside the dark silhouette at t = 36 s there is no cloud texture at all: the
clouds that cover the rest of the wall stop dead at the silhouette's edge. The only way to punch a
cloud-free hole in the cloud image is to stand in the projector's own beam. So it is the
projector's light that is being blocked, and that projector must therefore be above the arm.

**The same downward displacement shows up again on the performers themselves.** At about t = 86 s
the shadow of the love-symbol microphone stand lands on the lead singer's white dress *lower* than
the symbol itself, and offset to the right. Wherever a person is in shot, the crown of the head and
the tops of the shoulders are the brightest parts of them and the area under the chin and under the
brow is in shadow, which is the signature of light arriving from overhead.

**The metalwork is lit on its top edges.** On the horizontal boom arms around the drum kit at
t = 86–88 s, and on the isolated microphone at t = 88 s, the bright specular highlights run along
the *upper* edge of each tube and the undersides are dark. A light source below the performers
would put those highlights on the *lower* edges instead.

**The projected image also lands on the stage floor.** In the wide shots at t = 86–88 s, and again
at t = 228 s when the house lights come up, the same soft, wispy cloud texture that covers the wall
is clearly visible lying flat across the deck in front of the band, not only on the back wall.
Light can only fall onto a floor from something above that floor. A projector positioned below the
performers physically could not lay its picture down on the stage surface; it would throw
everything upwards. The spill on the floor is on its own sufficient to fix the projectors overhead,
and it also tells us they are angled steeply down, which is why the beam overshoots the bottom of
the wall and runs out onto the deck.

**There are shadows lying on the floor as well as on the wall.** In the wide lightning shot at
t = 185 s the microphone stand's tripod and the guitarist's legs each throw a dark shadow across
the deck they are standing on. An object can only cast a shadow onto the floor beneath it if the
light reaching it is coming from above; a source below the performers cannot put a shadow under
their own feet.

## Why there are two projectors

**The image is far too wide for one machine.** The picture is one continuous scene that covers the
whole back wall *and* carries on around onto the angled side returns at both ends of the set. This
is easiest to see in the shot at t = 142–144 s, where a bright horizontal band of the graphic runs
unbroken across the back wall and then continues onto the left-hand and right-hand angled walls,
where it appears larger and noticeably softer because those surfaces sit at a different throw
distance and so fall outside the lens's focal plane. Covering that whole wrap-around span from a
studio-length throw is beyond a single projector; it is exactly what you get from a pair of
machines, each doing roughly half the set.

**The wall has two brightness lobes with a fixed valley between them.** This is the strongest
quantitative evidence. I measured the horizontal brightness profile of a clean strip of the wall
above everybody's heads across six frames spanning three seconds of one continuous wide shot
(t = 85.6, 86.2, 86.8, 87.4, 88.0, 88.6 s). Every one of the six frames has the same structure: a
bright lobe on the left, a second bright lobe on the right, and a distinct dim valley in between —
and that valley sits at *exactly the same horizontal position* in all six frames even though the
cloud picture is visibly drifting sideways through it the whole time. A dark band that stays put
while the image moves through it cannot be part of the image; it has to be a property of the
lighting. Repeating the same measurement at four different heights up the wall in one frame
(t = 86 s) puts the valley at the same horizontal position every time, so the dim zone is not a
local patch but a vertical band running the full height of the wall, with a brighter region on
either side of it. Two bright lobes separated by a stable vertical trough is the footprint of two projectors whose
beams meet and blend near the centre of the wall, each one brightest under its own lens and falling
off towards the seam. The same twin-lobed profile with a central dip is measurable again in the
final wide shot at t = 228 s, under completely different lighting and content. A single projector
would instead give one broad hotspot, brightest in the middle and falling away evenly to both
edges, which is not what the wall does.

**The shadow directions require a source that is off to one side, and the coverage requires
another.** The shadows that are clearly readable — the sequinned sleeve at t = 36 s and the
love-symbol stand at t = 86 s — are both thrown down *and to the right*. A shadow pushed to the
right of its object can only be made by a source that is up and to the *left* of that object, and
since both of these objects are already on the left-hand side of the stage, the source making them
must be well up and to the left of the stage centre-line. A single projector parked that far to one
side would light the wall at a steep oblique angle and the right-hand half of the wall would fall
off badly in brightness and be visibly keystoned. It does not: the right-hand half of the wall is
independently bright and carries its own separate brightness lobe. Something else has to be
lighting it, from up and to the right. That is the second projector.

**How the shadows support the count, and one honest limit.** With two overlapping beams, any object
standing in the middle of the wall is lit from two directions at once, so each of its two shadows is
partly filled in by the other projector and neither one ever goes fully black. That is exactly the
pattern the footage shows: the shadows around the drum kit and mic stands in the middle of the wall
(t = 86–88 s) are soft, grey and low-contrast, whereas the one shadow that falls near the left-hand
edge of the wall — the sequinned sleeve at t = 36 s, out where only the left-hand projector really
reaches — is by a wide margin the hardest-edged and blackest shadow in the video. Shadows that
weaken in the middle of the wall and strengthen towards the outside are what a blended pair of
projectors produces; a single projector would give one hard shadow per object everywhere.

The limit worth stating plainly: at this resolution (720 x 404, heavily compressed) I could not
actually resolve two cleanly separated shadow copies of one single object and count them by eye.
The double-shadow pair is below the resolving power of this footage. So the count of two rests on
the coverage geometry, on the measured twin-lobe brightness structure with its fixed central
valley, and on the way the shadows soften in the overlap region and harden outside it, rather than
on literally counting two silhouettes of one object. The *direction* of the shadows, which is what
fixes the projectors above rather than below the performers, is directly visible and is not in
doubt.

# Where the background images come from

The three successive backdrops behind the band — first a bright cloudy sky (about 60–90 s in, e.g. the wide shot around 89 s), then a dark star field (about 118–128 s, e.g. the singer with outstretched arms around 121 s), then purple lightning (about 178–225 s) — are video images front-projected onto the back wall. The clouds visibly drift between frames, so this is a moving video image, not a painted cloth. There is a brief transitional pattern of two horizontal glowing blue bands at about 141–145 s.

## Projector position and number

The projectors are off-screen below the performers: two video projectors sitting at floor level in front of the stage, left and right of centre, shining upward and backward onto the backdrop and edge-blended to cover its width. They are not above the performers.

## How the shadows show this

Anything standing between a projector and the wall — a performer's head and torso, a microphone stand, a cymbal — blocks that projector's beam and throws a shadow onto the wall on the far side of the object from the projector.

- The shadows fall above the objects, not below them. In the bright cloudy-sky wide shots the clearest case is a large, soft, head-and-shoulders-shaped shadow looming high on the wall up and to one side of the backup singers (e.g. the big dark blob at the upper left of the wide frame around 118 s), far above any physical head. In the blue-band transition around 143–144 s each performer's torso punches a dark gap in the lower glowing band that is wider than the body itself, i.e. a magnified shadow thrown upward onto the wall, while the upper band passes uninterrupted above their heads. A source above the performers would instead throw shadows downward onto the floor or the low wall, and no such downward shadows appear anywhere.
- There are two shadows per object, not one. The shadow thrown high on the wall is doubled: a pair of soft, slightly offset shadows splaying upward and outward from each head, mic, and stand, overlapping into a single wider dark region close above the performer and separating higher up. One projector could only cast one shadow per object; the paired, diverging shadows require two spaced sources. This matches the wide-stage coverage (one unit cannot cover the whole wall) and the bright wash of projector light on the stage floor in front of the performers in the wide shots, with fixtures visible low at the frame edge.
- The effect is strongest when the projectors dominate the light (the dark blue-band passage, where the performers go almost pure black silhouette against the projected bands) and softest when stage wash competes, which is exactly what front-projection shadows do.

So: below the performers, two projectors, proven by doubled shadows cast upward onto the wall behind and above the people and hardware blocking the beams.
